<pasted_content id="48f3">
J'ai tout ce qu'il faut. Voici le texte à donner tel quel à l'autre Claude.

---

**Written for: an engineer implementing a G-code previewer in a separate application, who has no access to this codebase.**

## Contexte

Ce G-code est produit par un script Python autonome (`scripts/gen_elbow_tube_gcode.py`, sans dépendance externe) pour une imprimante 3D **4 axes maison** appelée Apex : 3 axes linéaires/polaires + 1 axe de rotation de tête. Ce n'est **pas** un G-code de slicer classique (Marlin/RepRap XYZ) — un prévisualiseur générique le rendra faux s'il traite X/Y/Z comme du cartésien standard.

## Format des lignes

Chaque mouvement est une ligne unique :

```
G00 Y<C> X<R> Z<Z> B<B> [E<e>] F<f>
```

- **X = R** : rayon depuis le centre du plateau, en mm. Toujours ≥ 0.
- **Y = C** : angle de rotation du plateau, en **degrés**, en repère absolu — **pas borné à [0, 360)**. La valeur peut dépasser 360° ou être négative ; c'est intentionnel (voir plus bas), jamais un bug à corriger en repliant la valeur.
- **Z** : hauteur, en mm, cartésien classique.
- **B** : inclinaison de la tête d'impression, en degrés. B=0 = buse verticale pointant vers le bas. B augmente = la buse penche **vers le centre du plateau** (vers −R). Plage observée : 0° à 45° dans ce script, mais la machine réelle va jusqu'à 185°.
- **E** (optionnel) : position absolue d'extrudeur, en mm de filament. Présent seulement sur les segments qui déposent de la matière. Son absence signale un déplacement à vide.
- **F** : vitesse, en mm/min, comme d'habitude — mais voir la remarque sur son calcul plus bas, qui peut surprendre un lecteur habitué aux slicers classiques.

Il n'y a **aucune autre commande de déplacement** (pas de G1/G2/G3), aucun G28/G29/nivellement, aucune commande plateau chauffant dans la configuration courante, et pas de rétraction (aucun G10/G11, aucun retrait de E avant un trajet à vide — limite connue, pas un oubli de votre côté).

## Conversion vers un repère cartésien affichable

Pour afficher la pièce, il faut reconstruire une position 3D à partir de (R, C, Z) :

```
x = R * cos(C en radians)
y = R * sin(C en radians)
z = Z
```

C'est une transformation polaire standard — la seule subtilité est que **C n'est jamais réduit modulo 360**, donc convertissez-le en radians directement sans le normaliser d'abord.

## Pourquoi C peut dépasser 360° ou être négatif (à ne pas "corriger")

Le générateur maintient une continuité angulaire : chaque nouveau C est recalé au plus proche de l'ancien C (`C_nouveau += ou -= 360` jusqu'à être à moins de 180° du précédent), pour éviter qu'un contour qui franchit ±180° ne fasse faire un tour complet inutile au plateau réel. Un fichier sain de ce générateur a un C qui **oscille dans une plage étroite** (typiquement moins de 40° d'amplitude totale sur toute la pièce) — jamais des dizaines de tours cumulés. Si votre previewer voit un C qui dérive sur des milliers de degrés, c'est le signe d'un fichier généré par une version bogguée du script (documentée en interne comme "le défaut de septembre"), pas une caractéristique normale du format.

## Ce qu'il faut représenter visuellement

1. **Le plateau tourne**, la matière déposée est donc solidaire de sa rotation : un point déposé à l'angle C1 doit apparaître, à un instant où le plateau est à l'angle courant C2, tourné de (C2 − C1) par rapport à sa position de dépôt. Concrètement : convertissez chaque point déposé en repère plateau `(R, angle_piece = C_au_moment_du_depot)` une fois pour toutes, puis à l'affichage, appliquez la rotation courante du plateau à **tous** les points en même temps pour obtenir leur position machine instantanée. Ne fixez jamais la pièce dans un repère "dérotaté" en ignorant la rotation plateau : elle est la caractéristique visuelle centrale de ce type de machine — visible dans notre propre prévisualiseur, où le plateau et la matière tournent ensemble, jamais dans des sens opposés (une erreur de signe qu'on a commise et corrigée : voir que les deux DOIVENT tourner strictement synchronisés, sinon la pièce apparaît en miroir).

2. **La tête n'a que 2 degrés de liberté de position (R, Z)** : elle se déplace uniquement dans un **demi-plan vertical fixe** de la machine (à un instant donné, elle n'est jamais "à côté" en Y machine — c'est le plateau qui tourne pour amener chaque point de la pièce sous elle). Représentez-la comme un segment ou une forme simple partant de (R, 0, Z) dans le repère machine, penchée de l'angle B vers −R (vers l'axe de rotation).

3. **Distinguer dépôt et trajet à vide** : segments avec E croissant = extrusion (à colorer/afficher pleins) ; segments sans E ou avec E stationnaire = déplacement à vide (à afficher en pointillé ou masqués par défaut, avec une option pour les montrer).

4. **Interpoler entre les points commandés**, pas seulement les afficher en escalier : le firmware interpole linéairement entre deux consignes (R, C, Z) — pas entre les positions cartésiennes (x,y,z) qui en résultent. Pour une animation fluide, faites l'interpolation dans le même espace (R, C, Z, B) que le firmware, puis convertissez le résultat en cartésien pour l'affichage, sinon la trajectoire simulée divergera de la trajectoire réelle dès que le plateau tourne pendant le mouvement.

## Deux pièges numériques déjà rencontrés en écrivant notre propre viewer

- **La densité de points compte plus que la résolution d'écran.** Une trajectoire de plateau oscillant sur seulement ±20° peut avoir un pas angulaire de 0.4° entre points consécutifs sur les portions courbes (coude) ; sous-échantillonner agressivement (par ex. garder 1 point sur 3) fait apparaître des sauts angulaires visibles de plusieurs degrés d'une image à l'autre. Gardez tous les points si le volume le permet, ou décimez avec un seuil sur l'écart angulaire/spatial max entre points consécutifs, jamais un simple "1 point sur N".
- **Le champ B n'est pas un simple angle de caméra.** Si la tête a un pivot de rotation qui n'est pas exactement à la pointe de la buse (cas réel rencontré ici), la position affichée de la pointe dépend aussi de B — mais ceci est déjà compensé dans les valeurs R/Z du G-code lui-même par notre générateur (paramètre `--pivot`) : le previewer n'a **rien à faire de spécial** pour ça, il doit juste afficher R/Z tels quels. Ne réappliquez pas de compensation de pivot côté previewer sauf si vous simulez explicitement une tête ayant son propre décalage pivot→pointe distinct de celui utilisé à la génération.

## Résumé en une phrase

C'est un G-code polaire (R, C, Z, B) où C est un angle absolu non replié qui doit rester dans une petite plage oscillante, et où la seule façon correcte de visualiser la pièce est de faire tourner ensemble, de façon synchronisée, à la fois les repères du plateau et la matière déjà déposée, pendant que la tête reste confinée à son demi-plan vertical.
</pasted_content id="48f3">

Utiliser cette documentation pour créer un prévisualisateur de code G dans l'espace Prévisualisation. L'espace Prévisualisation peut accepter le Drag & Drop de fichiers gcode, gco, g et ngc.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Project overview

Apex is a 3D printer slicer UI developed by Aelox Hardware: a Babylon.js viewport (build plate, printer boundary shader, model loading/manipulation) surrounded by shadcn/ui panels for file management, printer/filament config, texture editing, and slicing. This repo was originally scaffolded from the `vite_react_shadcn_ts` template — expect those scaffolding conventions (see AI_RULES.md) alongside hand-written slicer-specific code.

## Commands

```bash
pnpm install       # this repo uses pnpm (pnpm-lock.yaml / pnpm-workspace.yaml present)
pnpm dev           # vite dev server on port 8080
pnpm build         # production build
pnpm build:dev     # development-mode build
pnpm lint          # eslint .
pnpm preview       # preview the production build
```

There is no test runner configured in this repo (no test script, no test files).

## Architecture

### Global event bus, not shared state

There is no state management library and no shared React context between the sidebar/panel components and the 3D viewport. Instead, `Viewport3D.tsx` and every panel component communicate exclusively through `window.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent(...))` / `window.addEventListener(...)`, using a fixed set of `apex-*` event names, e.g.:

- `apex-tool-changed` — Sidebar → Viewport3D (select/move/rotate/scale/delete tool switch)
- `apex-mesh-selected`, `apex-mesh-deleted` — Viewport3D → ModelStatusBox, SliceSidebar, SliceModal, TextureEditorModal
- `apex-model-hover` — Viewport3D → ModelHoverTooltip
- `apex-import-model` — Sidebar → Viewport3D; Viewport3D → ModelStatusBox/SliceSidebar
- `apex-camera-updated` — Viewport3D → ViewCube (camera orientation sync)
- `apex-set-camera-view`, `apex-set-camera-custom`, `apex-reset-camera`, `apex-fit-screen` — panels/ViewCube → Viewport3D
- `apex-axis-changed` — AxisSidebar → SliceModal
- `apex-request-textures`, `apex-textures-loaded` — TextureEditorModal ↔ Viewport3D
- `apex-set-tooltip`, `apex-reset-tooltip` — CustomTooltip → TopRightMenu

When adding a feature that needs to move data between the viewport and any panel, follow this pattern rather than introducing prop drilling, context, or a store. When adding a new event, grep for `apex-` across `src/components` first to check whether an existing event already carries the needed data.

### Viewport3D is a self-contained Babylon.js engine

`src/components/Viewport3D.tsx` owns the entire Babylon.js lifecycle in a single `useLayoutEffect`: engine/scene/camera creation, the printer build-volume boundary (custom GLSL shader material defined inline via `BABYLON.Effect.ShadersStore`, radius/height constants at the top of the file), mesh import (`babylonjs-loaders` for GLB/STL), gizmo-based move/rotate/scale tools, mesh picking/highlighting, and hover/selection broadcasting. It holds all Babylon state in refs (`engineRef`, `sceneRef`, `cameraRef`, `gizmoManagerRef`, `modelsRef`, `selectedMeshesRef`) rather than React state, since Babylon objects are mutable and not meant to trigger re-renders. React state is only used for the few bits that need to affect JSX (e.g. `selectedMeshName`).

### Component/style structure

- `src/pages/Index.tsx` is the single page and composes every top-level panel; routing lives in `src/App.tsx` (React Router, per AI_RULES.md keep routes there).
- Feature panels (`Sidebar`, `FileSidebar`, `CategoriesSidebar`, `PrinterConfigSidebar`, `SliceSidebar`, `SliceModal`, `TextureEditorModal`, `AxisSidebar`, `TopRightMenu`, `ViewCube`, `ModelStatusBox`, `ModelHoverTooltip`) each pair with a `*.module.scss` file for custom styling (glassmorphism panels, custom sliders/drag handles) — Tailwind is used for layout/spacing, SCSS modules for bespoke visual treatment that Tailwind utilities don't cover.
- `src/components/ui/*` is generated shadcn/ui code — per AI_RULES.md, don't edit these directly; wrap or compose new components instead.
- Path alias `@/*` maps to `src/*` (configured in both `vite.config.ts` and `tsconfig.json`); shadcn aliases (`@/components`, `@/lib`, `@/hooks`, `@/components/ui`) are defined in `components.json`.
- Toast notifications go through `src/utils/toast.ts` (`showSuccess`/`showError` wrapping `sonner`), not direct `sonner` calls.

## Conventions from AI_RULES.md

- New pages go in `src/pages/`, new components in `src/components/`; routes are declared in `src/App.tsx`.
- Prefer shadcn/ui (`src/components/ui`) + Radix primitives + Tailwind for any new UI; all shadcn dependencies are already installed.
- After adding a component to `Index.tsx`'s tree, it must actually be rendered there or it won't be visible — keep the main page in sync with new components.

**Runtime capabilities** (optional): depending on what is enabled for this user, a published page can do more than static HTML — read the user's live or connected data, remember what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — the page saves new versions of itself), keep state shared across viewers, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question of its own, store files people add, or hand the viewer a file to save — declared via the `capabilities` input. **Whenever the user asks for a page that needs any of that, you MUST load the `artifact-capabilities` skill BEFORE writing the artifact, and always before passing `capabilities` or writing any `window.claude.*` runtime code** — it tells you what's available to this user and how to use it. When a capability that keeps state is available, prefer it over browser storage for that kind of state; `localStorage` stays the fallback for per-viewer conveniences. Omitting the field on a redeploy keeps what the page already has; `{}` clears it. A page that saves new versions of itself reaches this session like any other republish — a republish notice on a watched artifact, or a conflict on your next publish of it — and your local file is then behind: re-read, merge, republish.

action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai URL. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, which must be one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"); Claude omits it for a new artifact or a redeploy in the same conversation (see **To update an artifact from an earlier conversation**). For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

This tool runs Git Bash (POSIX sh), not cmd.exe or PowerShell. Use Unix shell syntax: `/dev/null` not `NUL`, forward slashes, `$VAR` not `%VAR%` or `$env:VAR`. Do not use PowerShell here-strings (`@'…'@`) or backtick continuation here — for multi-line strings use a heredoc.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

schema.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. Reads a file from the local filesystem.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch

Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

content.text:
L'espace Prévisualisation affiche maintenant un prévisualisateur de G-code polaire. On peut y glisser-déposer un fichier `.gcode`, `.gco`, `.g` ou `.ngc`, ou cliquer pour en choisir un. Le build, le typage et le lint passent, mais je ne l'ai pas encore essayé dans le navigateur avec un vrai fichier de `gen_elbow_tube_gcode.py` : c'est le test qui reste à faire.

(Pour votre « Pourtant si » : oui, le bouton Prévisualisation existait déjà. Il n'avait simplement aucun contenu, c'est ce que j'ai branché dessus.)

**Ce qui a été fait :**
- **Nouveau composant** [GCodePreview.tsx](src/components/GCodePreview.tsx) et son [SCSS](src/components/GCodePreview.module.scss). Il a sa propre scène Babylon, séparée de Viewport3D.
- **Lecture du fichier** : seules les lignes `G00` sont prises en compte, avec X = R, Y = C, Z, B et E. Un segment compte comme extrusion seulement si E augmente ; sinon c'est un trajet à vide. C n'est jamais ramené entre 0 et 360°.
- **Plateau et pièce tournent ensemble** : la matière est rattachée au même nœud que le plateau, donc une seule rotation les fait tourner exactement en même temps. J'ai vérifié le sens de rotation avec Babylon : un point déposé se retrouve pile sous la tête, puis il est entraîné par le plateau. Avec le signe inverse, la pièce apparaîtrait en miroir, le piège décrit dans la doc.
- **Tête** : elle reste dans son demi-plan fixe à (R, 0, Z) et la buse penche de B vers le centre (vérifié aussi). J'affiche R et Z tels quels, sans recalculer le décalage du pivot.
- **Tracé et animation** : les positions sont calculées en R, C, Z et B comme le fait le firmware, puis converties pour l'affichage. Les segments sont découpés par pas de 0,5° maximum pour suivre la vraie courbe, et aucun point n'est supprimé.
- **Fluidité** : la géométrie est construite une seule fois au chargement. Le curseur et la lecture ne font que choisir quelle portion de la trajectoire afficher, même avec de gros fichiers.
- **Interface** :
  - Un panneau d'infos (plage de Z, plage de C, et R/C/Z/B à la position courante), placé là où se trouvent d'habitude les catégories, qui sont masquées dans cet espace.
  - Une barre de lecture en bas : lecture/pause, curseur, vitesse en mouvements par seconde, et un bouton pour afficher les trajets à vide (masqués par défaut).
- **Fichier suspect** : si C varie de plus de 720° sur l'ensemble du fichier, un avertissement signale qu'il vient probablement de la version boguée du générateur (« le défaut de septembre »).
- **[Index.tsx](src/pages/Index.tsx)** : le prévisualisateur démarre à la première ouverture de l'espace. Ensuite il est seulement caché, et son affichage s'arrête : le fichier chargé est conservé si on change d'espace puis qu'on revient. La barre de statut du bas est cachée en Prévisualisation.

**À noter :**
- **Vitesse de lecture** : elle est fixe, en mouvements par seconde, et ne suit pas F. La doc annonce une remarque sur le calcul de F mais ne la donne jamais, donc je ne l'ai pas utilisé pour le temps.
- **Tracé des trajets à vide** : ils sont en gris semi-transparent plutôt qu'en pointillés, car Babylon ne propose pas de pointillés simples pour ce type de tracé.
- **Performances** : Viewport3D continue de s'afficher sous l'aperçu opaque, ce qui consomme du GPU pour rien. Il faudrait le mettre en pause dans cet espace, mais je n'y ai pas touché.

content.text:
Le tracé G-code est maintenant rendu dans la scène de Préparation elle-même. Plateau, grille, disque en verre flouté, contours cyan et caméra sont donc strictement les mêmes. Le typage, le lint et le build passent, et le tracé a été vérifié dans une scène Babylon hors écran avec un G-code d'essai (détails plus bas). Je ne l'ai pas encore ouvert dans le navigateur avec votre fichier.

**Ce que j'ai changé :** au lieu de recopier le décor dans une seconde scène, le tracé est affiché directement dans celle de [Viewport3D.tsx](src/components/Viewport3D.tsx).

- **[gcodeLayer.ts](src/components/gcodeLayer.ts)** (nouveau) : la lecture du fichier et la construction 3D du tracé et de la tête, sorties de l'ancien composant.
- **[Viewport3D.tsx](src/components/Viewport3D.tsx)** :
  - Le tracé est posé sur la surface du plateau, qui est surélevé. En Prévisualisation, les modèles de Préparation sont masqués puis réaffichés en ressortant, sans être modifiés.
  - Le tracé est exclu du flou du disque en verre : il aurait fait un halo autour des lignes et doublé leur coût de rendu.
- **[GCodePreview.tsx](src/components/GCodePreview.tsx)** : il ne garde que l'interface (dépôt de fichier, panneau d'infos, barre de lecture). Il communique avec le viewport par trois nouveaux événements : `apex-gcode-loaded`, `apex-gcode-time` et `apex-gcode-show-travel`. Il est transparent pour la souris, donc la caméra se manipule comme en Préparation. Le dépôt de fichier marche sur toute la fenêtre quand l'espace est actif.

**Test du tracé :** j'ai chargé un G-code d'essai où C va de 350° à 370°, donc franchit 360°. Le fichier est bien lu et C n'est pas ramené entre 0 et 360°. Les trajets à vide sont bien masqués par défaut. Le curseur de lecture affiche la bonne portion du tracé. Le dernier point déposé tombe pile sous la tête.

**Conséquence visible :** le plateau étant un disque uni, sa rotation ne se voit pas. C'est la matière qui montre la rotation. Si vous voulez un repère sur le plateau (un trait à 0° par exemple), je peux l'ajouter, mais cela ferait une différence avec la Préparation.

**À noter :** j'ai aussi renommé le nouveau module `gcodePreview.ts` en `gcodeLayer.ts`. Windows ignore la casse des noms de fichiers : `@/components/GCodePreview` aurait pu être résolu vers ce module au lieu du composant.

Quel est le point suivant sur votre liste ?
L'animation point par point ne fonctionne pas : quand on fait glisser le curseur vers la gauche, ça ne change pas. De plus, le bouton Play ne fait rien.

Le curseur et le bouton Play fonctionnent maintenant. Je l'ai vérifié dans Chrome, piloté par un script, avec un G-code de test en hélice. Glisser le curseur vers la gauche fait reculer le tracé, et Play fait avancer la pièce et la tête.

Il y avait deux bugs distincts :

1. **Le rendu plantait** dès qu'on affichait moins que le tracé complet, avec l'erreur `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'boundingSphere')`. La boucle de rendu Babylon s'arrêtait alors et l'image restait figée, alors que les commandes du curseur et de Play arrivaient bien. Babylon a besoin d'une zone englobante pour chaque morceau dessiné du tracé, et je ne la créais pas pour un tracé partiel. Au chargement, tout le tracé est affiché, donc le bug n'apparaissait qu'au premier retour en arrière. Mon test hors écran de la dernière fois ne vérifiait pas le dessin lui-même, c'est pour ça qu'il ne l'avait pas vu. La correction est dans [gcodeLayer.ts](src/components/gcodeLayer.ts) : cette zone est créée une seule fois au chargement.
2. **Le curseur ne recevait pas la souris** : la barre d'aide centrée en bas de l'écran ([TopRightMenu](src/components/TopRightMenu.tsx)) se trouvait au-dessus de lui. J'ai remonté la barre de lecture juste au-dessus de cette barre d'aide.

Pour les tests, j'ai installé un outil de pilotage de Chrome (`playwright-core`) dans le dossier temporaire, pas dans le projet. Le port 8080 était déjà occupé, sans doute par votre serveur de dev : je ne l'ai pas touché et j'ai lancé le mien sur 8093, puis je l'ai arrêté.

Quel est le point suivant ?

message.content:
This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
## 1. Demande principale et intention

- **Demande de départ.** L'utilisateur a fourni une documentation détaillée (en français) du G-code polaire 4 axes de l'Apex, généré par `scripts/gen_elbow_tube_gcode.py`. Il veut qu'on s'en serve pour créer un prévisualisateur G-code dans l'espace **Prévisualisation** existant, avec glisser-déposer de fichiers `.gcode`, `.gco`, `.g` et `.ngc`.
- **Points clés de la documentation :**
  - Lignes du type `G00 Y<C> X<R> Z<Z> B<B> [E<e>] F<f>`. X = R (rayon), Y = C (angle du plateau en degrés, absolu, **jamais ramené modulo 360**), B = inclinaison de la tête vers −R, E optionnel (E croissant = extrusion).
  - Plateau et matière tournent strictement ensemble. Une erreur de signe fait apparaître la pièce en miroir.
  - La tête reste dans un demi-plan vertical fixe, à (R, 0, Z).
  - Interpoler dans l'espace (R, C, Z, B), pas en cartésien.
  - Pas de décimation « 1 point sur N ».
  - Ne pas réappliquer de compensation de pivot : R et Z sont affichés tels quels.
  - Un C qui dérive sur des milliers de degrés signale un fichier issu du générateur bogué (« le défaut de septembre »).
- **Retour 1 :** l'espace Prévisualisation existe bien déjà (« Pourtant si »).
- **Retour 2 :** l'apparence de l'espace 3D (plateau et grille) doit être identique à celle de l'espace Préparation.
- **Retour 3 :** le curseur ne change rien quand on le fait glisser vers la gauche, et le bouton Play ne fait rien.
- L'utilisateur avait annoncé « Plusieurs trucs qui ne vont pas » : d'autres points peuvent suivre.

## 2. Concepts techniques clés

- **Stack :** React, Vite, pnpm, Babylon.js 9.15 (paquet UMD `babylonjs`), SCSS modules, Tailwind, framer-motion, lucide-react.
- **Communication :** bus d'événements global `apex-*` via `window.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent(...))`, sans store ni context (règle de CLAUDE.md).
- **Babylon, repère main gauche :** `rotation.y = ψ` envoie l'angle local θ (x = cos θ, z = sin θ) sur θ − ψ. Avec ψ = +C courant, un point déposé tombe sous la tête (angle machine 0) au moment du dépôt. Vérifié numériquement.
- **Orientation de la tête :** `Quaternion.FromUnitVectorsToRef(Up, (-sinB, cosB, 0))`.
- **Tracé :**
  - `LinesMesh` construit à partir de `VertexData` brut (positions, couleurs, indices en paires).
  - Un préfixe du tracé s'affiche en modifiant `subMesh.indexCount` à partir d'un tableau cumulé `cumIndices` par mouvement.
  - Il faut `subMesh.setBoundingInfo` : dès que le sous-maillage n'est plus « global », Babylon lit sa boîte englobante propre.
- **Scène de Viewport3D :**
  - Plateau porté par `volumeRoot` (y = HEIGHT × 0.5), surface `glassDisc` à y local 0,1.
  - Disque « verre dépoli » flouté via `blurRT`, filtré par `capturedInBlur`.
  - Grille de fond : shader `backdrop`.
- **Superposition de l'interface :** conteneur en `pointer-events: none` (enfants en `auto`). Le glisser-déposer est écouté sur `window` quand l'espace est actif.
- **Pièges rencontrés :**
  - Windows ignore la casse : un import `GCodePreview` peut être résolu vers `gcodePreview.ts`.
  - TopRightMenu est en réalité une barre d'aide centrée en bas : `position: fixed`, `bottom: 24px`, `min-height: 44px`, z-index 1000.

## 3. Fichiers et sections de code

### src/components/gcodeLayer.ts (nouveau, logique centrale)

Il exporte :
- les types `GCodeMove { r, c, z, b, extruding }` et `ParsedGCode { moves, minZ, maxZ, maxR, minC, maxC, extrudingCount }` ;
- `parseGCode(text)`, `stateAt(moves, t)` ;
- `SUSPICIOUS_C_RANGE_DEG = 720` ;
- `GCODE_MESH_PREFIX = 'gcode'` ;
- l'interface `GCodeLayer` et `createGCodeLayer(scene, parent)`.

**Parseur.** Il retire les commentaires `(...)` et `;`, ne traite que les lignes G00 (`/^G0*0(?![0-9])/i`) et lit les mots avec `/([XYZBEF])\s*([-+]?(?:\d+\.?\d*|\.\d+))/gi`. Les valeurs sont modales. Règle d'extrusion : `extruding = e !== null && lastE !== null && e > lastE + 1e-9`.

**`stateAt`.** Interpolation linéaire de r, c, z et b entre `moves[floor(t)]` et le mouvement suivant.

**`buildPathMesh(name, parsed, segments, wantExtruding, colorAt, scene)`.**
- Chaque mouvement correspondant est subdivisé en `segments[k]` morceaux (`ceil(|ΔC| / 0.5°)`, au moins 1), avec positions `(r cos c, z, r sin c)`.
- Il crée `new BABYLON.LinesMesh(name, scene, null, null, undefined, true, true)` et applique le `VertexData`.
- **Correctif :**
  ```ts
  const { minimum, maximum } = mesh.getBoundingInfo();
  mesh.subMeshes[0].setBoundingInfo(new BABYLON.BoundingInfo(minimum.clone(), maximum.clone()));
  ```
- `isPickable = false`, `alwaysSelectAsActiveMesh = true`. Il renvoie `{ mesh, cumIndices }`.

**`createGCodeLayer`.**
- **Nœuds :** `gcodeRoot` (parent : le paramètre `parent`, désactivé au départ), `gcodePlate` (nœud tournant, parent de tout le tracé) et `gcodeHead`.
- **Tête :** buse orange `gcodeNozzle` (diameterTop 7, diameterBottom 0.6, height 9, position.y 4.5) et corps gris semi-transparent `gcodeHeadBody` (diameter 14, height 26, y 22).
- **`apply()` :**
  - `plateNode.rotation.y = state.c * DEG2RAD` ;
  - `headNode.position.set(r, z, 0)` et orientation de la tête par quaternion ;
  - pour les maillages extrusion et trajet à vide : `count = cumIndices[i]`, plus la partie en cours `floor((t - i) * segments[next]) * 2` si le mouvement suivant est du même type ; puis `sub.indexCount = count` et `mesh.isVisible = count > 0`.
- **`load(parsed)` :**
  - supprime les anciens tracés et calcule `segments` ;
  - couleurs : dégradé selon Z de (0.1, 0.45, 1) à (0.3, 0.95, 1) pour l'extrusion, (0.8, 0.8, 0.85, 0.35) pour les trajets à vide ;
  - rattache les tracés à `plateNode`, masque les trajets à vide selon `showTravel`, active la tête, place `time` sur le dernier mouvement et appelle `apply()`.
- **Autres méthodes :** `setTime`, `setShowTravel`, `setEnabled` (sur root), `dispose`.

### src/components/GCodePreview.tsx (interface seule)

- **Props :** `{ active: boolean }`. Le composant renvoie `null` quand il est inactif mais reste monté, ce qui conserve son état.
- **Constantes :** `SPEED_OPTIONS = [25, 100, 400, 1600, 6400]` (mouvements par seconde), `ACCEPTED_EXT = /\.(gcode|gco|g|ngc)$/i`.
- **Événements émis :**
  - `apex-gcode-loaded` `{ parsed }` au chargement ;
  - `apex-gcode-time` `{ t }`, via `dispatchTime`, depuis `seek` et à chaque image de lecture ;
  - `apex-gcode-show-travel` `{ show }`.
- **Horloge de lecture :** un effet `requestAnimationFrame` sur `[isPlaying, speed]` fait avancer `tRef` de `speed * dt`, émet à chaque image et met à jour le state React à environ 20 Hz.
- **Chargement :** `loadFile` valide l'extension et parse le fichier. S'il y a moins de 2 mouvements, il affiche une erreur. Si la plage de C dépasse 720°, `showWarning` signale un fichier probablement issu du générateur bogué ; sinon `showSuccess`.
- **Glisser-déposer :** écouteurs `dragenter`, `dragover`, `dragleave` et `drop` sur `window`, uniquement quand l'espace est actif, avec un compteur de profondeur.
- **Lecture :** `togglePlay` revient à 0 si la lecture est déjà à la fin.
- **Interface :**
  - bouton central vide « Glissez un fichier G-code ici » ;
  - superposition pendant le dépôt ;
  - panneau d'infos (nom, nombre de mouvements, dont extrusion, hauteur, plage de C, R/C/Z/B courants, badge du segment, « Ouvrir un autre fichier… ») ;
  - barre de lecture (Play/Pause avec `aria-label` « Lecture »/« Pause », curseur range de 0 à `lastIndex` par pas de 0,01, libellé, sélecteur de vitesse, bouton « Trajets à vide »).

### src/components/GCodePreview.module.scss

- Mixin `glass-panel`.
- `.container` : `absolute; inset: 0; z-index: 15; pointer-events: none`, enfants `> *` en `pointer-events: auto`.

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Project overview

Apex is a 3D printer slicer UI developed by Aelox Hardware: a Babylon.js viewport (build plate, printer boundary shader, model loading/manipulation) surrounded by shadcn/ui panels for file management, printer/filament config, texture editing, and slicing. This repo was originally scaffolded from the `vite_react_shadcn_ts` template — expect those scaffolding conventions (see AI_RULES.md) alongside hand-written slicer-specific code.

## Commands

```bash
pnpm install       # this repo uses pnpm (pnpm-lock.yaml / pnpm-workspace.yaml present)
pnpm dev           # vite dev server on port 8080
pnpm build         # production build
pnpm build:dev     # development-mode build
pnpm lint          # eslint .
pnpm preview       # preview the production build
```

There is no test runner configured in this repo (no test script, no test files).

## Architecture

### Global event bus, not shared state

There is no state management library and no shared React context between the sidebar/panel components and the 3D viewport. Instead, `Viewport3D.tsx` and every panel component communicate exclusively through `window.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent(...))` / `window.addEventListener(...)`, using a fixed set of `apex-*` event names, e.g.:

- `apex-tool-changed` — Sidebar → Viewport3D (select/move/rotate/scale/delete tool switch)
- `apex-mesh-selected`, `apex-mesh-deleted` — Viewport3D → ModelStatusBox, SliceSidebar, SliceModal, TextureEditorModal
- `apex-model-hover` — Viewport3D → ModelHoverTooltip
- `apex-import-model` — Sidebar → Viewport3D; Viewport3D → ModelStatusBox/SliceSidebar
- `apex-camera-updated` — Viewport3D → ViewCube (camera orientation sync)
- `apex-set-camera-view`, `apex-set-camera-custom`, `apex-reset-camera`, `apex-fit-screen` — panels/ViewCube → Viewport3D
- `apex-axis-changed` — AxisSidebar → SliceModal
- `apex-request-textures`, `apex-textures-loaded` — TextureEditorModal ↔ Viewport3D
- `apex-set-tooltip`, `apex-reset-tooltip` — CustomTooltip → TopRightMenu

When adding a feature that needs to move data between the viewport and any panel, follow this pattern rather than introducing prop drilling, context, or a store. When adding a new event, grep for `apex-` across `src/components` first to check whether an existing event already carries the needed data.

### Viewport3D is a self-contained Babylon.js engine

`src/components/Viewport3D.tsx` owns the entire Babylon.js lifecycle in a single `useLayoutEffect`: engine/scene/camera creation, the printer build-volume boundary (custom GLSL shader material defined inline via `BABYLON.Effect.ShadersStore`, radius/height constants at the top of the file), mesh import (`babylonjs-loaders` for GLB/STL), gizmo-based move/rotate/scale tools, mesh picking/highlighting, and hover/selection broadcasting. It holds all Babylon state in refs (`engineRef`, `sceneRef`, `cameraRef`, `gizmoManagerRef`, `modelsRef`, `selectedMeshesRef`) rather than React state, since Babylon objects are mutable and not meant to trigger re-renders. React state is only used for the few bits that need to affect JSX (e.g. `selectedMeshName`).

### Component/style structure

- `src/pages/Index.tsx` is the single page and composes every top-level panel; routing lives in `src/App.tsx` (React Router, per AI_RULES.md keep routes there).
- Feature panels (`Sidebar`, `FileSidebar`, `CategoriesSidebar`, `PrinterConfigSidebar`, `SliceSidebar`, `SliceModal`, `TextureEditorModal`, `AxisSidebar`, `TopRightMenu`, `ViewCube`, `ModelStatusBox`, `ModelHoverTooltip`) each pair with a `*.module.scss` file for custom styling (glassmorphism panels, custom sliders/drag handles) — Tailwind is used for layout/spacing, SCSS modules for bespoke visual treatment that Tailwind utilities don't cover.
- `src/components/ui/*` is generated shadcn/ui code — per AI_RULES.md, don't edit these directly; wrap or compose new components instead.
- Path alias `@/*` maps to `src/*` (configured in both `vite.config.ts` and `tsconfig.json`); shadcn aliases (`@/components`, `@/lib`, `@/hooks`, `@/components/ui`) are defined in `components.json`.
- Toast notifications go through `src/utils/toast.ts` (`showSuccess`/`showError` wrapping `sonner`), not direct `sonner` calls.

## Conventions from AI_RULES.md

- New pages go in `src/pages/`, new components in `src/components/`; routes are declared in `src/App.tsx`.
- Prefer shadcn/ui (`src/components/ui`) + Radix primitives + Tailwind for any new UI; all shadcn dependencies are already installed.
- After adding a component to `Index.tsx`'s tree, it must actually be rendered there or it won't be visible — keep the main page in sync with new components.
